top_results.snippet: 老大昌与它对角的国泰电影院一样，一脚茂名南路一脚淮海路，而门牌挂的是淮海中路877号。名叫“洋行”，做的是法式面包和点心生意。老板后为法国人查卡利（F.Tchakalian），改名查卡利面包糖果公司（Tchakalian Bros French Bakery），叫起来拗口，听上去吃力；遂改“老大昌法国面包房”。西头这家叫“老大昌面包房”，1945年转中国人经营。1956年，法国老板回国，法国老大昌也转华商。两家合并。

top_results.snippet: 老大昌创办于1903年，法国远东商业公司在法租界公馆马路开设食品商店，中文名叫老大昌。1919年老板换成亚美尼亚人皮埃尔·察卡利安（Pierre Tchakalian），后外文店名多次变更，最终为“Tchakalian Bros' French Bakery”。1935年其旗舰店一分为二，东边877号由皮埃尔经营，西边873-875号由堂兄约瑟夫经营，共用“老大昌”店名。1945年877号转让给中国商人朱砚清，称“华商老大昌”。

top_results.title: 细水微焰丨光陆大戏院——商场影院的百年光芒
top_results.snippet: 光陆大戏院，位于博物馆路（现虎丘路）南苏州路口。由英商斯文洋行投资，设计师是当时在上海滩与邬达克齐名的匈牙利籍建筑师鸿达，1925年动工，1928年2月25日落成开幕。钢筋混凝土结构，平面成扇形。Artdeco装饰艺术派风格。1930年代，光陆大戏院曾放映迪士尼动画片，鲁迅先生是这里的常客。1941年，太平洋战争爆发后，剧场被汪伪中华电影公司强行管辖，改名叫“文化电影院”。抗战胜利后由原业主收回，恢复“Capitol”名称。1951年由上海市文化局接管，1954年改名曙光剧场，1955年改为专映科教电影，1964年划归市外贸局使用。如今这里成为外滩源的一部分，光陆大楼即将百年之际，很快就将重新绽放。

{"url": "https://researchomnia.blogspot.com/2024/12/italian-tripoli-libya.html", "status_code": 200, "title": "Researchomnia: ITALIAN TRIPOLI (LIBYA)", "text": "Researchomnia: ITALIAN TRIPOLI (LIBYA)
Thursday, December 5, 2024
ITALIAN TRIPOLI (LIBYA)
This month I am going to research the "Italian Tripoli", capital of Italian Libya from 1911 to 1947.
Italian Tripoli was the capital of "Italian Libya". During the early XX century the city of Tripoli was under Italian control for 3 decades, that lasted from 1911 until January 1943. Italians conquered the town of less than 20,000 inhabitants from the Ottoman empire and enlarged it in 1943 to a big city of nearly 120,000 "Tripolini" (more than half Italians), creating a vibrant and modern capital in north Africa.
The census of 1939 showed this population in Tripoli:
Town......	Italians.......	Arabs........ Jews........ Total
Tripoli...	 47,442.........	47,123......  18,467......113,212
Italian Tripoli was at the center of Italian NorthAfrica in the "Greater Italy" during WW2 (borders in orange color).With Decree of 9 January 1939 the four provinces of Tripoli, Misurata, Benghazi and Derna were aggregated to the Kingdom of Italy, becoming an integral part of the Italian metropolitan territory.
History
During the Italo-Turkish War of 1911 Tripoli was conquered by the Italian Kingdom. The Italian fleet appeared off Ottoman Tripoli in the evening of September 28, 1911: the city was quickly conquered by 1,500 Italian sailors, welcomed by the population (
https://archive.org/details/tripoliitalianal00mart/page/36/mode/2up
Tripoli inhabitants welcomed the Italians; p. 36-40). The huge jewish community of Tripoli was very supportived of the Italian occupation (
http://archive.diarna.org/site/detail/public/1784/
).
TRIPOLI ITALIANA: The Grand Hotel, built in the early 1930
With the 1912 treaty signed in Ouchy, Italian sovereignty was acknowledged by the Ottomans, although the local Caliph was permitted to exercise religious authority. Italy officially granted autonomy after the war, but gradually occupied the region of Tripolitania. Originally administered as part of a single colony, Tripoli and its surrounding province were a separate colony from 26 June 1927 to 3 December 1934, when all Italian possessions in North Africa were merged into one colony called ''Libia''.
Since 1937 the governor Italo Balbo started a policy of immigration of Italians (mainly farmers) who were called the Ventimilli and some of them settled in the area of Italian Tripoli (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N_jA9rzM1MsVideo of Italian settlers arriving in the port of Tripoli).
Fiat train "Littorina" at Tripoli station
So, by the end of 1937, the city had 108,240 inhabitants, including 39,096 Italians (according to The Statesman's Yearbook 1948. Palgrave Macmillan. p. 1040). At the start of WWII Italian Tripoli had 111,124 inhabitants of which the Italians were 41,304: 37% of the city's inhabitants. Additionally there were nearly 18,000 Jews in the Tripoli area. Indeed after the Italian occupation of Libya in 1911, the Jews made great strides in education and economic conditions: at that time, there were about 21,000 Jews in the country, the majority in Tripoli. In the late 1930s, Fascist anti-Jewish laws were gradually enforced, and Jews were subject to moderate repression: still, by late 1940 -due even to the partial rejection of those laws by governor Italo Balbo- the Jews accounted for a fifth of the population of Tripoli and maintained 44 synagogues.
In 1942 Tripoli -according to estimates of the Italian government (Istituto Agricolo Coloniale (Firenze); Ministero degli Esteri, 1946)- reached a temporary population of nearly 150,000 inhabitants, due to the arrival of many Italians from Benghazi and Cyrenaica who took refuge from the British army attacks during WWII. As a consequence Tripoli was in that year -for the first time since the Arab conquest in 643 AD- a city mostly Christian.
Fiera internazionale di Tripoli ("Tripoli International Fair") in 1939
Architectural and Urbanistic improvement of Italian Tripoli
Tripoli underwent a huge architectural and urbanistic improvement under Italian rule (http://www.fedoa.unina.it/1881/1/Santoianni_Progettazione_Architettonica.pdf Tripoli section: p. 54-59). The first thing the Italians did was to create in the early 1920s a sewage system (that until then lacked) with water & electrical facilities to all the city and a modern hospital. Also was started the creation of the modern port.
Furthermore, in the western section of Tripoli was created an industrial area in the 1930s, around a huge tobacco factory (called "Manufattura Tabacchi di Tripoli"), with railway workshops, Fiat Motor works, various food processing plants, electrical engineering workshops, ironworks, water plants, agricultural machinery factories, breweries, distilleries, biscuit factories, tanneries, bakeries, lime, brick and cement works.
Governor Balbo used to say that "We Italians found in 1911 a big village of approximately 20,000 inhabitants called Tripoli and now we have in 1940 a modern capital nearly ten times bigger and one of the most developed and vibrant cities of Africa". (photos of Tripoli: http://www.paolocason.eu/Viaggio%20a%20Tripoli.htm ).
In the coast of the province was built in 1937-1938 a section of the Litoranea Balbia, a road that went from Tripoli and Tunisia's frontier to the border of Egypt. The car tag for the Italian province of Tripoli was "TL" (Berionne, Michele. "Libia (1937-1943)"  Italian car tags )
Furthermore the Italians - in order to promote Tripoli's economy - founded in 1927 the "Tripoli International Fair", which is considered to be the oldest Trade Fair in Africa (http://tripolifair.com/tripoli-international-fair/ Tripoli International Fair brief history). The so-called Fiera internazionale di Tripoli was one of the main international "Fairs" in the colonial world in the 1930s, and was internationally promoted together with the Tripoli Grand Prix as a showcase of Italian Libya(http://cronologia.leonardo.it/storia/a1937f.htm Filippo Giannini: Colonial Italy and Islam (in Italian).
Italian Tripoli's Via Generale De Bono in 1933
Indeed the Italians even created the "Tripoli Grand Prix", an international motor racing event first held in 1925 on a racing circuit outside Tripoli that lasted until 1940 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KEtz-wzbs9YVideo of Tripoli Grand Prix).Tripoli during the Grand Prix was visited by the elite tourism of the world and had even some "fashion" shops (
https://www.pinterest.com/pin/187040190754209597/
Italian women walking near the Tripoli Castle in 1939).
The first airport in Libya, the "Mellaha Air Base" was built by the Italian Air Force in 1923 near the Tripoli racing circuit (actually is called "Mitiga International Airport"). The regular air services (with postal services) in Libya began in November 1928 with the first Rome-Syracuse-Tripoli air route, three times a week in winter, daily in summer, of the "Societa Anonima Navigazione Aerea (SANA)" airplanes. In the December of 1931 the "Società Nord Africa Aviazione (NAA)" inaugurated the Benghazi-Agedabia-Sirte-Tripoli line, which followed the coast line. With the absorption of the two companies from the ''Ala Littoria'' in 1935 the service continued on the same routes. From 4 April 1937 the Rome-Tunis line of Ala Littoria was extended to Tripoli; in 1938 the Air France opened a Marseilles-Tripoli line, then extended to Benghazi and Damascus. (
www.academia.edu/2326842/
Le Poste italiane fuori dI'talia).
Tripoli had even a modern railway station with some small railway connections to nearby cities, when in August 1941 the Italians started to build a new 1,040 kilometres (646 miles) railway (with a 1,435 mm (56.5 in) gauge, like the one used in Egypt and Tunisia) between Tripoli and Benghazi. But the war -with the defeat of the Italian Army- stopped the construction the next year: only one hundred miles were created, but it was done also the project to connect this new railway with the borders of Tunisia & Egypt.
Banca d'Italia in 1932
Tripoli was controlled by Italy until 1943 when the provinces of Tripolitania and Cyrenaica were captured by Allied forces. The city fell to troops of the British Eighth Army on 23 January 1943 and the Italian colonists since then started to diminish (the following photo shows a family of farm colonists with British soldiers).
Tripoli was then governed by the British until independence in 1951. Under the terms of the 1947 peace treaty with the Allies, Italy relinquished all claims to Libya.
After WWII the era of international decolonization fostered a huge exodus of Italians from Tripoli (
http://intranet.istoreto.it/esodo/parola.asp?id_parola=25
https://books.google.com/books?id=ax0EpcZqeMkC&pg=PA12&lpg=PA12&dq=gheddafi+expulsion+of+italians&source=bl&ots=OYfkJX6Gd-&sig=7jgJ5We-toLe59m-eIyoYaBjjik&hl=en&sa=X&ei=PMEyVJnpE9C8ggSbzYGIBg#v=onepage&q=gheddafi%20expulsion%20of%20italians&f=false.  Gaddafi expulsion of the Italians in 1970).
At present, the Libyan Italians are organized in the Associazione Italiani Rimpatriati dalla Libia (. http://www.airl.it Associazione Italiani Rimpatriati dalla Libia). The remaining "Tripolini" struggle to get their confiscated properties (http://www.airl.it/la-nostra-storia#eventistorici  History of the Italian refugees from Gheddafi Libya) and even to maintain their Italian cemetery (
www.corriere.it/esteri/16_aprile_10/cimitero-italiano-tripoli-sterpaglie-croci-divelte-devastazioni-70e3480c-ff61-11e5-a032-8e8dfe3b8a86.shtml
Attacks on the Tripoli Italian Cemetery)
Infrastructures
Since the first years in Italian Tripoli were made many infrastructures by the Italians, even with the participation of the local arab "elite" (Journal of Libyan Studies 3, 1 (2002) p. 59-68: "Local Elites and Italian Town Planning Pr

trace.payload_to_model:
{"url": "https://researchomnia.blogspot.com/2024/12/italian-tripoli-libya.html", "status_code": 200, "title": "Researchomnia: ITALIAN TRIPOLI (LIBYA)", "text": "Researchomnia: ITALIAN TRIPOLI (LIBYA)
Thursday, December 5, 2024
ITALIAN TRIPOLI (LIBYA)
This month I am going to research the "Italian Tripoli", capital of Italian Libya from 1911 to 1947.
Italian Tripoli was the capital of "Italian Libya". During the early XX century the city of Tripoli was under Italian control for 3 decades, that lasted from 1911 until January 1943. Italians conquered the town of less than 20,000 inhabitants from the Ottoman empire and enlarged it in 1943 to a big city of nearly 120,000 "Tripolini" (more than half Italians), creating a vibrant and modern capital in north Africa.
The census of 1939 showed this population in Tripoli:
Town......	Italians.......	Arabs........ Jews........ Total
Tripoli...	 47,442.........	47,123......  18,467......113,212
Italian Tripoli was at the center of Italian NorthAfrica in the "Greater Italy" during WW2 (borders in orange color).With Decree of 9 January 1939 the four provinces of Tripoli, Misurata, Benghazi and Derna were aggregated to the Kingdom of Italy, becoming an integral part of the Italian metropolitan territory.
History
During the Italo-Turkish War of 1911 Tripoli was conquered by the Italian Kingdom. The Italian fleet appeared off Ottoman Tripoli in the evening of September 28, 1911: the city was quickly conquered by 1,500 Italian sailors, welcomed by the population (
https://archive.org/details/tripoliitalianal00mart/page/36/mode/2up
Tripoli inhabitants welcomed the Italians; p. 36-40). The huge jewish community of Tripoli was very supportived of the Italian occupation (
http://archive.diarna.org/site/detail/public/1784/
).
TRIPOLI ITALIANA: The Grand Hotel, built in the early 1930
With the 1912 treaty signed in Ouchy, Italian sovereignty was acknowledged by the Ottomans, although the local Caliph was permitted to exercise religious authority. Italy officially granted autonomy after the war, but gradually occupied the region of Tripolitania. Originally administered as part of a single colony, Tripoli and its surrounding province were a separate colony from 26 June 1927 to 3 December 1934, when all Italian possessions in North Africa were merged into one colony called ''Libia''.
Since 1937 the governor Italo Balbo started a policy of immigration of Italians (mainly farmers) who were called the Ventimilli and some of them settled in the area of Italian Tripoli (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N_jA9rzM1MsVideo of Italian settlers arriving in the port of Tripoli).
Fiat train "Littorina" at Tripoli station
So, by the end of 1937, the city had 108,240 inhabitants, including 39,096 Italians (according to The Statesman's Yearbook 1948. Palgrave Macmillan. p. 1040). At the start of WWII Italian Tripoli had 111,124 inhabitants of which the Italians were 41,304: 37% of the city's inhabitants. Additionally there were nearly 18,000 Jews in the Tripoli area. Indeed after the Italian occupation of Libya in 1911, the Jews made great strides in education and economic conditions: at that time, there were about 21,000 Jews in the country, the majority in Tripoli. In the late 1930s, Fascist anti-Jewish laws were gradually enforced, and Jews were subject to moderate repression: still, by late 1940 -due even to the partial rejection of those laws by governor Italo Balbo- the Jews accounted for a fifth of the population of Tripoli and maintained 44 synagogues.
In 1942 Tripoli -according to estimates of the Italian government (Istituto Agricolo Coloniale (Firenze); Ministero degli Esteri, 1946)- reached a temporary population of nearly 150,000 inhabitants, due to the arrival of many Italians from Benghazi and Cyrenaica who took refuge from the British army attacks during WWII. As a consequence Tripoli was in that year -for the first time since the Arab conquest in 643 AD- a city mostly Christian.
Fiera internazionale di Tripoli ("Tripoli International Fair") in 1939
Architectural and Urbanistic improvement of Italian Tripoli
Tripoli underwent a huge architectural and urbanistic improvement under Italian rule (http://www.fedoa.unina.it/1881/1/Santoianni_Progettazione_Architettonica.pdf Tripoli section: p. 54-59). The first thing the Italians did was to create in the early 1920s a sewage system (that until then lacked) with water & electrical facilities to all the city and a modern hospital. Also was started the creation of the modern port.
Furthermore, in the western section of Tripoli was created an industrial area in the 1930s, around a huge tobacco factory (called "Manufattura Tabacchi di Tripoli"), with railway workshops, Fiat Motor works, various food processing plants, electrical engineering workshops, ironworks, water plants, agricultural machinery factories, breweries, distilleries, biscuit factories, tanneries, bakeries, lime, brick and cement works.
Governor Balbo used to say that "We Italians found in 1911 a big village of approximately 20,000 inhabitants called Tripoli and now we have in 1940 a modern capital nearly ten times bigger and one of the most developed and vibrant cities of Africa". (photos of Tripoli: http://www.paolocason.eu/Viaggio%20a%20Tripoli.htm ).
In the coast of the province was built in 1937-1938 a section of the Litoranea Balbia, a road that went from Tripoli and Tunisia's frontier to the border of Egypt. The car tag for the Italian province of Tripoli was "TL" (Berionne, Michele. "Libia (1937-1943)"  Italian car tags )
Furthermore the Italians - in order to promote Tripoli's economy - founded in 1927 the "Tripoli International Fair", which is considered to be the oldest Trade Fair in Africa (http://tripolifair.com/tripoli-international-fair/ Tripoli International Fair brief history). The so-called Fiera internazionale di Tripoli was one of the main international "Fairs" in the colonial world in the 1930s, and was internationally promoted together with the Tripoli Grand Prix as a showcase of Italian Libya(http://cronologia.leonardo.it/storia/a1937f.htm Filippo Giannini: Colonial Italy and Islam (in Italian).
Italian Tripoli's Via Generale De Bono in 1933
Indeed the Italians even created the "Tripoli Grand Prix", an international motor racing event first held in 1925 on a racing circuit outside Tripoli that lasted until 1940 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KEtz-wzbs9YVideo of Tripoli Grand Prix).Tripoli during the Grand Prix was visited by the elite tourism of the world and had even some "fashion" shops (
https://www.pinterest.com/pin/187040190754209597/
Italian women walking near the Tripoli Castle in 1939).
The first airport in Libya, the "Mellaha Air Base" was built by the Italian Air Force in 1923 near the Tripoli racing circuit (actually is called "Mitiga International Airport"). The regular air services (with postal services) in Libya began in November 1928 with the first Rome-Syracuse-Tripoli air route, three times a week in winter, daily in summer, of the "Societa Anonima Navigazione Aerea (SANA)" airplanes. In the December of 1931 the "Società Nord Africa Aviazione (NAA)" inaugurated the Benghazi-Agedabia-Sirte-Tripoli line, which followed the coast line. With the absorption of the two companies from the ''Ala Littoria'' in 1935 the service continued on the same routes. From 4 April 1937 the Rome-Tunis line of Ala Littoria was extended to Tripoli; in 1938 the Air France opened a Marseilles-Tripoli line, then extended to Benghazi and Damascus. (
www.academia.edu/2326842/
Le Poste italiane fuori dI'talia).
Tripoli had even a modern railway station with some small railway connections to nearby cities, when in August 1941 the Italians started to build a new 1,040 kilometres (646 miles) railway (with a 1,435 mm (56.5 in) gauge, like the one used in Egypt and Tunisia) between Tripoli and Benghazi. But the war -with the defeat of the Italian Army- stopped the construction the next year: only one hundred miles were created, but it was done also the project to connect this new railway with the borders of Tunisia & Egypt.
Banca d'Italia in 1932
Tripoli was controlled by Italy until 1943 when the provinces of Tripolitania and Cyrenaica were captured by Allied forces. The city fell to troops of the British Eighth Army on 23 January 1943 and the Italian colonists since then started to diminish (the following photo shows a family of farm colonists with British soldiers).
Tripoli was then governed by the British until independence in 1951. Under the terms of the 1947 peace treaty with the Allies, Italy relinquished all claims to Libya.
After WWII the era of international decolonization fostered a huge exodus of Italians from Tripoli (
http://intranet.istoreto.it/esodo/parola.asp?id_parola=25
https://books.google.com/books?id=ax0EpcZqeMkC&pg=PA12&lpg=PA12&dq=gheddafi+expulsion+of+italians&source=bl&ots=OYfkJX6Gd-&sig=7jgJ5We-toLe59m-eIyoYaBjjik&hl=en&sa=X&ei=PMEyVJnpE9C8ggSbzYGIBg#v=onepage&q=gheddafi%20expulsion%20of%20italians&f=false.  Gaddafi expulsion of the Italians in 1970).
At present, the Libyan Italians are organized in the Associazione Italiani Rimpatriati dalla Libia (. http://www.airl.it Associazione Italiani Rimpatriati dalla Libia). The remaining "Tripolini" struggle to get their confiscated properties (http://www.airl.it/la-nostra-storia#eventistorici  History of the Italian refugees from Gheddafi Libya) and even to maintain their Italian cemetery (
www.corriere.it/esteri/16_aprile_10/cimitero-italiano-tripoli-sterpaglie-croci-divelte-devastazioni-70e3480c-ff61-11e5-a032-8e8dfe3b8a86.shtml
Attacks on the Tripoli Italian Cemetery)
Infrastructures
Since the first years in Italian Tripoli were made many infrastructures by the Italians, even with the participation of the local arab "elite" (Journal of Libyan Studies 3, 1 (2002) p. 59-68: "Local Elites and Italian Town Planning Pr

Name of Monument:
Hammouda Pacha Mosque
Location:
Tunis medina, Tunisia
Responsible Institution (original language):
Ministère des Affaires religieuses
Date of Monument:
18th century
History:
This mosque was built on top of the kasbah by the Muradid sovereign, Hammouda Pacha Bey, in the 17th century, and was modelled on the Turkish mosque built by Youssef Dey near the Sidi Ahmed Ben Arous
zawiya
on the intersection between Rue Sidi Ben Arous and the kasbah. The mosque is also located near the Great Zaytuna Mosque, which gave these new Hanafi masters some legitimacy.
Description:
The Hammouda Pacha Mosque is an example of a new type of architecture, with a square floor and a pyramid roof with green tiles. The décor is rich and varied, featuring many panels in carved stucco and marquetery, with alternating motifs on a black and white marble base, and elements of baroque decorations can be seen on the façade of the
tourba
. Other innovative elements include a V-shaped courtyard, an octagonal minaret and a mausoleum (tourbet). This mausoleum marked the opening of the first funerary mosque in Tunis, which creates a link between the place of worship and the founder's tomb.
Citation of this web page:
Saloua Khadhar Zangar "Hammouda Pacha Mosque " in "Sharing History", Museum With No Frontiers, 2026.

trace.content:
¡Excelente! La imagen 3 muestra el minarete de la mezquita Hammouda Pacha en Túnez. Es octagonal, con una galería en la parte superior, y tiene una forma MUY similar al minarete de la foto target. La estructura octagonal, los patrones decorativos, y la galería con arcos son consistentes.

Ahora comparo:
- **Foto target**: minarete octagonal con zigzag, dos niveles de galería, decoración elaborada
- **Hammouda Pacha (Tunis)**: minarete octagonal, similar estilo otomano

La similitud es fuerte. Además, Tunis tenía un "Ospedale Italiano" (fundado 1890, llamado Garibaldi desde 1907). El minarete de Sidi Youssef Dey (1615) fue el primero octagonal en Tunis y sirvió de modelo para el de Hammouda Pacha.

Busquemos la ubicación exacta del ospedale italiano en la medina de Tunis y si estaba cerca de estas mezquitas.

trace.content:
Ahora tengo información crucial. El "Ospedale coloniale italiano" en Tunis estaba en la "rue Zaouia El Bokria" dentro de la medina, establecido en 1890. La mezquita Hammouda Pacha con su minarete octagonal está en la Rue Sidi Ben Arous, y el minarete de la Sidi Youssef Dey (1615, octagonal) está cerca. 

El minarete de la foto con sus patrones zigzag decorativos y forma octagonal encaja perfectamente con los minaretes otomanos de Tunis. La presencia del cartel "OSPEDALE ITALIANO" dentro de la medina concuerda con el hospital italiano que existió en la medina de Tunis desde 1890.

Ahora verifiquemos visualmente con Street View cerca de la mezquita Hammouda Pacha.

Name of Monument:
Yussef Dey Mosque
Location:
At the entrance to the town on the
kasbah
side, Tunis, Tunisia
Date of Monument:
Hegira 1020 / AD 1612
Architect(s) / master-builder(s):
Ibn Ghaleb al-Andalusi.
Period / Dynasty:
Husaynid-Ottoman
Patron(s):
Yussef Dey.
History:
After the annexation of Ifriqiya to the Ottoman Empire in the 10th / 16th century the number of Hanefite-rite Turks grew constantly. Two Malekite mosques, the Kasbah Mosque and the al-Qsar Mosque, were then given over to the Hanefite rites. Then Yussef Dey decided to give Tunis its first Turkish mosque. The works were commenced in 1023 (1614) and finished one year later.
Description:
The
mosque
bears the name of its founder and is particularly interesting because, while preserving several features of the Ifriqiyan
mosque
, it introduces several architectural novelties in its layout and construction.
The prayer hall is no longer set behind a single courtyard, but framed with courtyards on the eastern, western and northern sides. Along the north façade, the portico serves as a substitute for the narthex in local mosques. An octagonal
minaret
rises from a square base at the north-west corner. At the top is a balcony with a wooden awning, above which there is a lantern turret with a pyramidal roof covered with green tiles. This octagonal tower was to serve as a model for al-Jadid
Mosque
and for the
Mosque
of Yussef Sahib al- Taba'a.
The mausoleum, or
turbe
, built along the façade, is the first example in Tunis of a funerary
mosque
where the tomb of the founder is associated with the place of worship. The tomb of Yussef
Dey
is built on a square plan and has a pyramidal roof with green tiles. On each face is a large central arcature, flanked by two storeys of sunken niches with flat rear walls. The corner columns set on both levels considerably lighten the mass. The white marble flooring is enhanced with alternating blocks of black and white. The date of the
turbe
is inscribed on the central arcature.
The innovations, that is to say, the U-shaped courtyard, the octagonal
minaret
and the addition of the
turbe
, are outside the prayer hall. The prayer hall perpetuates the classic layout of the rectangular, pillared hall with nine naves and seven bays. The central nave and the bay parallel to the
qibla
wall are larger than the others and, at their meeting point, form a T-shape in front of the
mihrab
. The columns are of several types but, apart from a few ancient examples, all have Hafsid capitals. The roof is of groined vaults. At the front of the
mihrab
is an octagonal-based dome with scalloped pendentives.
The only new feature in this oratory is the stone-built
minbar
with its polychrome marble panelling. Malekite
minbars
are usually made of wood.
View Short Description
This was the first Turkish
mosque
in the Tunis
kasbah
, built in the early AH 11th / AD 17th century. With its square plan and green-tiled pyramid roof, this
mosque
, which was named after its founder, introduced a new style of architecture. The innovations include a U-shaped courtyard, an octagonal
minaret
and a mausoleum (
turbe
). This type of funerary
mosque
, in which the founder’s tomb was combined with a place of worship, was a Tunisian innovation.
How Monument was dated:
According to the inscription above the main entrance to the prayer hall, the works began on 10
Shawwal
1023 (13th November 1614) and went on until 22
Ramadan
(14th October 1024).

revue

Interesante hallazgo. El primer resultado menciona que el **Ospedale Coloniale Italiano** en Túnez estuvo primero en el **barrio de Halfaouine**, y luego se mudó cerca de **Bab el-Fellah** en 1900. En Túnez, el hospital italiano fue renombrado "Ospedale Giuseppe Garibaldi" en 1907. 

Pero en la foto veo "OSPEDALE ITALIANO" como nombre. Esto me hace pensar que puede ser el hospital de Trípoli, ya que el de Túnez cambió de nombre a "Garibaldi" en 1907. Sin embargo, "Ospedale Italiano" podría ser un nombre genérico que se usaba coloquialmente.

Debo centrarme en el minarete. El de la Mezquita Gurgi de Trípoli y el de la Mezquita Zitouna de Túnez son ambos octogonales. Voy a buscar específicamente el minarete de Halfaouine en Túnez (Mezquita Halfaouine/Sahib et-Taba'a) que está en el barrio donde estaba el hospital italiano.

Ahora puedo comparar detalladamente. El minarete de la Mezquita Gurgi (celdas 1 y 2) tiene:
- Forma octogonal
- Dos balcones con arcos
- Bandas verdes horizontales (mármol verde)
- Punta cónica con cúpula verde

Pero el minarete de mi foto target tiene:
- Forma octogonal similar
- Decoración con patrón **zigzag** muy prominente
- Un patrón de ladrillo más complejo con bandas geométricas
- Una sola balconada abierta grande (tipo galería)
- La punta tiene esferas/bolas debajo de la media luna

Los minaretes NO son idénticos. El de la foto target parece ser **más ornamentado con zigzag** y tiene un estilo diferente. Esto me hace reconsiderar - podría ser otro minarete en Trípoli (como el de Karamanli o Draghut) o podría ser en Túnez.

Voy a buscar específicamente minaretes con patrón zigzag en la medina de Trípoli.

trace.content:
Ahora puedo ver el minarete con mucho más detalle. Tiene:
1. **Media luna** en la punta con **3 esferas** debajo
2. Punta **cónica** con **almenas/merlones** alrededor
3. Una **galería abierta** con balcón techado (tipo cubierta con alero)
4. Debajo del balcón, una banda con **arcos pequeños ciegos** (muqarnas/corbels)
5. Un prominente patrón **zigzag** en la parte del fuste
6. **Ventanas arqueadas** (arcos de herradura)
7. Decoración geométrica circular/rosetones

Comparando con el minarete de la Mezquita Gurgi que vi en las fotos modernas: el Gurgi tiene bandas verdes lisas y un estilo más sencillo. El minarete de mi foto target es **mucho más ornamentado** con zigzag y rosetones.

Esto me hace pensar que podría ser la **Mezquita de Karamanli** o la **Mezquita de Sidi Hammouda** en Trípoli, o quizás una mezquita en **Túnez**. Déjame buscar más imágenes de minaretes específicos.

trace.content:
Tengo buena evidencia de la medina de Trípoli. Ahora la clave es: el hospital cerca de la mezquita "Assomaa Alhamra" (minarete rojo) en la calle Saidi. Esto es diferente de la Mezquita Gurgi. La "Assomaa Alhamra" es una mezquita con un **minarete rojo** cerca del hospital colonial. Y la descripción de Trek.zone confirmó que el minarete de la Mezquita Gurgi tiene un "zigzag pattern". 

Comparando el minarete de la foto target con el de la Mezquita Gurgi en las fotos modernas (celda 1 del zoom anterior), veo diferencias significativas. El de la foto target tiene más ornamentación y un balcón techado diferente.

Sin embargo, las fotos antiguas pueden mostrar el minarete de la Gurgi ANTES de restauraciones. La descripción habla de un patrón zigzag que efectivamente veo en mi foto target. La Gurgi está a 68m del Arco de Marco Aurelio, en el corazón de la medina.

Voy a verificar si el "Ospedale Italiano" podría haber estado en la medina, quizás distinto del gran hospital colonial. También buscaré la mezquita "Assomaa Alhamra".

{"url": "https://sannicolasantiguo.blogspot.com/2011/11/la-plaza-principal.html", "status_code": 200, "title": "San Nicolás Antiguo: La Plaza Principal", "text": "San Nicolás Antiguo: La Plaza Principal
La Plaza Principal
Fiesta escolar en la "Plaza Constitución" (actual Plaza Mitre) - 1891
"Para ver caras bonitas,
vé a la plaza por las noches ... "
(Periódico "Nene Pulgada" 1O - 1 - 1892)
La Plaza "Mitre" tiene en sí, el sello de las antiguas fundaciones de  pueblos. Nació con la organización del pueblo de San Nicolás de los  Arroyos, que tiene fecha oficializada de 14 de abril de 1748, y los  primeros pobladores la vieron delimitarse con la Capilla y el caserío  que, paulatinamente, se levantaba a su alrededor. Ellos, y la  instalación de las primeras dependencias públicas para los cuales Aguiar  donó los solares, le dieron fisonomía de importancia. Y fue desde  entonces, la "Plaza Principal".
Aún en esa condición -  posiblemente-, yucas y tunas, cina - cinas y garabatos señoreaban  todavía en su interior, mientras el verde pastizal era bien aprovechado  por cuanto ganado anduviese suelto por "el pago". Inclusive, el de la  misma hacienda del organizador que - es tradición- abrió esa "Bajada" al  río que hoy la acompaña en su esquina norte, obra manual rústica  entonces, que le permitió ofrecer una aguada natural a esa su riqueza,  que inició nuestra economía.
Y es posible, así mismo, que poco  después haya sido utilizada como lugar de descanso de las carretas, sus  "yuntas" y carreteros, que hicieron el transporte comercial de la  mercadería llegada por vía fluvial, al habilitarse el puerto, en el año  1823.
Entonces sigue siendo la plaza "principal" pues ya se  concentran en ella, aparte de la Capilla, de la residencia de los Aguiar  y del cementerio; la posta, el cuartel, escuela, cárcel, y más tarde la  Municipalidad instalada en 1854. Es decir, que se perfila y acrecienta  su importancia como escenario público.
En el decurso de su  existencia ha sido - y sigue siéndolo- escenario obligado de asambleas  políticas; de discursos que evocan a los forjadores de la patria; de  concentraciones cívicas; de profesión de fe religiosa; de  manifestaciones en pro de reivindicaciones sociales; pista circense; de  conciertos musicales; de inspiración para poetas; de expansión  espiritual para gente de todas las edades; de referencia ciudadana; en  fin, podemos decir, de innúmeras inquietudes de las que han forjado este  presente nuestro.
* Bibliografía: "Radiografía de San Nicolás  de los Arroyos" Tomo V - "Plaza Teniente General Bartolomé Mitre" La  "Plaza Principal" Creada por Rafael de Aguiar, por Gregorio Santiago  Chervo - 1983

trace.content:
Las celdas 7 y 8 muestran la Plaza Mitre de San Nicolás de los Arroyos en los años '50 - tiene jardines elaborados y palmeras pero el diseño es diferente al de mi foto target (más formal, con palmeras grandes y diseños geométricos). Mi foto parece ser de una época anterior, cuando la plaza tenía reja perimetral, faroles de gas/kerosene, y un diseño más informal con senderos curvos.

Sin embargo, la foto de la fiesta escolar de 1891 (celda 5) muestra la plaza con edificios de fondo que tienen arcos similares. Esto podría ser la misma plaza en una época anterior. Voy a buscar fotos más antiguas de la Plaza Mitre/Constitución de San Nicolás, y también explorar la Fototeca San Nicolás.

trace.content:
Veo que la Plaza Mitre actual en San Nicolás está rodeada de edificios modernos altos (torres de apartamentos), lo cual es muy diferente de la foto target que muestra edificios bajos coloniales. Pero eso es esperable - la ciudad creció mucho desde 1900. En la vista hacia el norte (heading=0) puedo ver un edificio histórico con columnas a la izquierda, y en la vista hacia el sur se ve la plaza con árboles grandes y palmeras, y lo que parece ser una iglesia a la izquierda (con una cruz).

La plaza actual no tiene reja perimetral, lo cual también es consistente - la reja fue removida en algún momento del siglo XX. Sin embargo, necesito considerar si la disposición general de la plaza y los edificios coincide con la foto antigua.

Su primer nombre fue «Plaza de la Constitución», impuesto en 1854, dado que allí se juró la Constitución provincial. Pero desde 1921 lleva el nombre de Bartolomé Mitre. Actualmente la Municipalidad emprendió su puesta en valor, obra que renovará el espacio público más histórico que tiene nuestra ciudad.
Epígrafe:
Las autoridades locales señalaron que la puesta en valor de la Plaza Mitre “le dará características modernas al lugar que convoca a todos los nicoleños”.
DANIEL DORADO/EL NORTE
De la Redacción de EL NORTE
[email protected]
La Plaza Mitre nació antes que la propia ciudad, puesto que era el espacio libre frente a las casas que componían la estancia del fundador. Cuando en 1748 queda constituida la ciudad, este sector libre recibió el nombre de «Plaza Principal». La parcela fue donada por el propio fundador Rafael de Aguiar.
En 1854 pasó a denominarse «Plaza de la Constitución», en virtud de que allí se juró la Constitución provincial. Desde 1921 lleva el nombre de Bartolomé Mitre. La plaza reúne una serie de monumentos y homenajes realizados por diferentes sectores. En el centro se erige el pequeño obelisco construido cuando la ciudad celebró los 250 años de su fundación. Frente al Club Social se erige el monumento a Juan Domingo Perón y Eva Duarte. También hay placas dedicadas a los soldados nicoleños que participaron en la Guerra del Paraguay, y una al pie del retoño del árbol de Guernica, símbolo de los vascos.
Primeros vecinos
Los primeros pobladores la vieron delimitarse con la capilla y el caserío que, paulatinamente, se levantaba a su alrededor. Ellos, y la instalación de las primeras dependencias públicas para las cuales Aguiar donó los solares, le dieron fisonomía de importancia. Y fue desde entonces la plaza central. Hasta el día de hoy es el lugar de referencia para todos, nicoleños y también ocasionales visitantes. No sólo porque en sus inmediaciones se ha desarrollado un fuerte componente comercial y de servicios, sino porque es el metro cero a partir del cual el nicoleño explica cómo llegar hasta el Santuario, dirigirse al paseo costanero o conocer algún edificio histórico y de interés turístico y religioso.
Obras y puesta en valor
Actualmente, la Municipalidad de San Nicolás se encuentra trabajando en la puesta en valor de la Plaza Mitre, obra que renovará el espacio público más histórico que tiene nuestra ciudad. Se está trabajando sobre las veredas en toda la manzana, las fuentes, el mobiliario y la reforestación.
Las autoridades locales señalaron que dicha puesta en valor “le dará características modernas al lugar que convoca a todos nicoleños y, a la vez, permitirá volver a posicionarla como una carta de presentación de la ciudad ante aquellos que la visitan”.
La obra también contempla luminarias led en todo su perímetro. Por otra parte, la reconstrucción de la plaza integra el acondicionamiento de la Bajada Belgrano.
Cabe recordar que los trabajos incluyen, además, la reconversión de la peatonal al sistema ‘manda-peatón’ que se encuentra en todo el centro, con veredas anchas para la gastronomía y la posibilidad de la circulación vehicular a baja velocidad, uniendo el centro con los miradores y la costanera.

{"url": "https://en.siauliuistorija.lt/2022/05/18/siauliai-streets-tell-stories-tilzes-street/", "status_code": 200, "title": "Šiauliai streets tell their stories. Tilžės Street - History of Šiauliai", "text": "Šiauliai streets tell their stories. Tilžės Street - History of Šiauliai
Šiauliai streets tell their stories. Tilžės Street
Tilžės Street is the longest street in the city, extending from Ginkūnai settlement to Lieporiai residential area and reaching about 11 kilometres. The Riga-Tilžė Highway built in the middle of the 19 century did not change the previous city plan formed as early as in 1783. The route was built across the square to the north, towards Riga. This way, two perpendicular axes were formed in the city centre, consisting of the current Vilniaus Street and the section of Riga-Tilžė Highway, which became part of one of the main streets of the city. That section of the road was called Šoseinaja ulica (Plento Street). In the plan of 1852, it is recorded as Tauragenskaja ulica (Tauragės Street). The street was named Sobornaja ulica (Soboro Street) in 1867, when next to the already standing St Apostles Peter and Paul’s Church, the Orthodox church was built. This name remained until World War I. During the war, the street in the city territory was not long, but the Germans divided it into two parts: Mitauer Strasse (Mintaujos Street) going in the direction of Riga and Tilsiter Strasse (Tilžės Street) going in the direction of Tilžė. In 1924, the street became unbroken again and was given the name Tilžės. The street grew longer and its names were changing. After World War II, it was called Tarybų, a bit later, Lenino, and eventually, the name Tilžės was returned to it.
The Chocolate Museum
In 1913, Antanas Gricevičius, a former employee of Vilnius Chocolate and Sweets Factory, established the Sweets Factory Rūta. He bought a large plot of land in the city centre with a garden and a house where he set up a sweets workshop. The factory was founded with only five workers. A. Gricevičius made sweets himself and took care of product advertising.
In 2012, the Sweets Factory Rūta, which was attracting passers-by by the sweet smells of chocolate, caramel, roasted nuts and boiled berries for almost a century, opened the door of its old building to visitors. Namely here, in the old building of the factory, the Chocolate Museum of Rūta was founded.
The exposition of the museum does not only present the interesting history of the factory but also reveals the secrets and peculiarities of four millennia of chocolate consumption.
Julius Janonis Gymnasium
In 1838, first efforts were made to set up a gymnasium in Šiauliai. Two plots of land were purchased for this purpose. Landlord I.Vitkevičius agreed to demolish the abandoned Pašiaušės Jesuit Church that belonged to him and until spring of 1845, to take its bricks to Šiauliai for the construction of the gymnasium.
In 1851, the solemn opening ceremony of Šiauliai Gymnasium took place. From the establishment of the gymnasium until World War I, it was called Šiauliai Boys’ Gymnasium.
In 1946, it was given the name Julius Janonis. Since 1954, the gymnasium is both for girls and boys. In 1965, it was granted a status of a gymnasium with a humanitarian profile.
Stained Glass Saulės mūšis (The Battle of the Sun)
The stained glass Saulės mūšis is in the Concert Hall Saulė (the former cinema). Three of the second floor lobby walls of the Soviet architectural building were adapted for the stained glass.
The stained glass that is 3,8 meters high, 52,1 meters long and occupies the area of 200 square meters was unveiled in 1986 to commemorate 750 years’ anniversary of Šiauliai city.
It is an impressive and majestic piece of art, the first monumental work of art of such theme and scale in the country. The stained glass is dedicated to the fight of ancient Lithuanians, it reveals tension and dramatism of that fight. Visual and colour rhythm of the stained glass sound solemnly, like organ music.
The building with a spacious lobby in front of the audience hall and its three glass walls – one front and two side walls – determined the compositional structure of the stained-glass.
The author of the stained glass, artist Kazys Morkūnas aimed to symbolically and artistically give a sense to the Battle of the Sun, disclose fighters’ heroism, strength, and determination.
St Apostles Peter and Paul’s Cathedral
The monument of Renaissance architecture St Peter and Paul’s Cathedral is the city’s most striking landmark. It as if shows the visitor where the city centre is.
The cathedral does not only dominate due to its impressive height (the apex of the tower reaches 70 meters) but also because of its convenient and well-chosen location.
The construction of the new church started around 1617. It is considered that it was initiated by the Samogitian bishop Mikalojus Pacas, while the key sponsor was the governor of Šiauliai Crown Estate Jeronimas Valavičius. Construction works were led by the dean of the church, the graduate of Vilnius Academy Petras Tarvainis.
On October 8, 1634, the bishop of Samogitia Jurgis Tiškevičius consecrated the new church of Šiauliai. Thanks to these people, a meaningful epithet “the greatest in all Samogitia”, describing the beauty and majesty of the church’s architecture, was heard on the lips of the Samogitian bishop Motiejus Valančius in later centuries.
Interestingly, the church tower had a mechanical clock installed for the money of the city residents.
The image of the architectural monument of the 17 century slightly changed over time. Wars and storms devastated the church time and again. Every few decades the church was repaired, renovated.
Prisikėlimo Square (Resurrection Square)
The central square of the city is divided into 4 parts by Aušros Avenue and Tilžės Street. This is the place around which the city of Šiauliai started growing. For centuries, the square was used for markets, fairs, live trading.
Interestingly, this oldest square of the city, the heart of the city, did not have an official name for a long time: it used to be called just Market, Market Square. Only in 1938, the square was assigned the name Laisvė (Freedom). In 1948, it was called Pergalė (Victory). In 1998, by the
decision of Šiauliai City Council, the city’s central square was labelled Prisikėlimo (Resurrection) in the honour of the Resurrection District of the Lithuanian partisans’ resistance, to which Šiauliai partisans also belonged. The square symbolizes the resurrection of the nation.

Muy bien. Ahora tengo una buena comprensión de Šiauliai. La calle Tilžės (antes Sobornaja ulica) era la calle principal norte-sur, y la postal de arkivi con la caballería alemana muestra la misma calle con la torre de la catedral de San Pedro y San Pablo al fondo. Mi foto target podría ser de una calle diferente - quizás Vilniaus gatvė (antes Fabričnaja ulica) u otra calle del centro.

Pero necesito considerar también que la foto podría no ser de Šiauliai sino de otra ciudad lituana o báltica. Déjame verificar si puedo encontrar la foto exacta o una muy similar buscando en otros archivos. También voy a considerar que podría ser Kaunas, Jelgava u otra ciudad.

Primero, déjame mirar más de cerca la foto para buscar más pistas - veo que hay un bloque blanco/gris en la parte inferior izquierda que podría ser un borde de postal con texto.

El día de la Fundación. Por orden cronológico, el 18 de Octubre de 1783  marca el comienzo de la vida institucional urbana, cuando Don Tomás de Rocamora deja constituida formalmente la  Villa al nombrar, con acuerdo de los vecinos, su primera institución de gobierno: el Cabildo de San José de Gualeguaychú.
En ese contexto histórico la plaza, constituyó el primer espacio urbano público, a cuyo alrededor se instalaron las primeras instituciones de la ciudad (capilla, cementerio, escuela, comandancia) y será escenario desde entonces y hasta el presente de numerosos acontecimientos de la vida comunitaria, en distintas circunstancias. Espacio que con el tiempo ha cambiado de nombres (originalmente Plaza de  Armas o Plaza Mayor (1783), luego Plaza Independencia (1879), hoy San Martín(1973) ) y también su fisonomía, pero no el protagonismo. El lugar ha sido y es punto de convocatoria para celebraciones religiosas, actos patrióticos, recreativos, artísticos o de protesta.
MONUMENTO AL GENERAL SAN MARTÍN:
El país se apresta a celebrar el centenario del 25 de Mayo de 1810. Gualeguaychú levantaría el primer monumento de la ciudad en la plaza principal, la estatua del General San Martín, obra del escultor Soatti. Su pedestal simulará una roca de granito artificial, con la base de 6 por 7 metros y una altura que se eleve de 4 a 5 metros. Se adosarán a él alegorías como la del Sol de Mayo y gran palma de bronce; una placa con el fragmento de “El nido de cóndores” de Olegario V. Andrade. Sobre la roca un cóndor y entre sus garras la bandera argentina.
La inauguración del monumento debió postergarse para el 29 de mayo de 1910.

{"url": "https://en.siauliuistorija.lt/2022/05/18/siauliai-streets-tell-stories-tilzes-street/", "status_code": 200, "title": "Šiauliai streets tell their stories. Tilžės Street - History of Šiauliai", "text": "Šiauliai streets tell their stories. Tilžės Street - History of Šiauliai
Šiauliai streets tell their stories. Tilžės Street
Tilžės Street is the longest street in the city, extending from Ginkūnai settlement to Lieporiai residential area and reaching about 11 kilometres. The Riga-Tilžė Highway built in the middle of the 19 century did not change the previous city plan formed as early as in 1783. The route was built across the square to the north, towards Riga. This way, two perpendicular axes were formed in the city centre, consisting of the current Vilniaus Street and the section of Riga-Tilžė Highway, which became part of one of the main streets of the city. That section of the road was called Šoseinaja ulica (Plento Street). In the plan of 1852, it is recorded as Tauragenskaja ulica (Tauragės Street). The street was named Sobornaja ulica (Soboro Street) in 1867, when next to the already standing St Apostles Peter and Paul’s Church, the Orthodox church was built. This name remained until World War I. During the war, the street in the city territory was not long, but the Germans divided it into two parts: Mitauer Strasse (Mintaujos Street) going in the direction of Riga and Tilsiter Strasse (Tilžės Street) going in the direction of Tilžė. In 1924, the street became unbroken again and was given the name Tilžės. The street grew longer and its names were changing. After World War II, it was called Tarybų, a bit later, Lenino, and eventually, the name Tilžės was returned to it.
The Chocolate Museum
In 1913, Antanas Gricevičius, a former employee of Vilnius Chocolate and Sweets Factory, established the Sweets Factory Rūta. He bought a large plot of land in the city centre with a garden and a house where he set up a sweets workshop. The factory was founded with only five workers. A. Gricevičius made sweets himself and took care of product advertising.
In 2012, the Sweets Factory Rūta, which was attracting passers-by by the sweet smells of chocolate, caramel, roasted nuts and boiled berries for almost a century, opened the door of its old building to visitors. Namely here, in the old building of the factory, the Chocolate Museum of Rūta was founded.
The exposition of the museum does not only present the interesting history of the factory but also reveals the secrets and peculiarities of four millennia of chocolate consumption.
Julius Janonis Gymnasium
In 1838, first efforts were made to set up a gymnasium in Šiauliai. Two plots of land were purchased for this purpose. Landlord I.Vitkevičius agreed to demolish the abandoned Pašiaušės Jesuit Church that belonged to him and until spring of 1845, to take its bricks to Šiauliai for the construction of the gymnasium.
In 1851, the solemn opening ceremony of Šiauliai Gymnasium took place. From the establishment of the gymnasium until World War I, it was called Šiauliai Boys’ Gymnasium.
In 1946, it was given the name Julius Janonis. Since 1954, the gymnasium is both for girls and boys. In 1965, it was granted a status of a gymnasium with a humanitarian profile.
Stained Glass Saulės mūšis (The Battle of the Sun)
The stained glass Saulės mūšis is in the Concert Hall Saulė (the former cinema). Three of the second floor lobby walls of the Soviet architectural building were adapted for the stained glass.
The stained glass that is 3,8 meters high, 52,1 meters long and occupies the area of 200 square meters was unveiled in 1986 to commemorate 750 years’ anniversary of Šiauliai city.
It is an impressive and majestic piece of art, the first monumental work of art of such theme and scale in the country. The stained glass is dedicated to the fight of ancient Lithuanians, it reveals tension and dramatism of that fight. Visual and colour rhythm of the stained glass sound solemnly, like organ music.
The building with a spacious lobby in front of the audience hall and its three glass walls – one front and two side walls – determined the compositional structure of the stained-glass.
The author of the stained glass, artist Kazys Morkūnas aimed to symbolically and artistically give a sense to the Battle of the Sun, disclose fighters’ heroism, strength, and determination.
St Apostles Peter and Paul’s Cathedral
The monument of Renaissance architecture St Peter and Paul’s Cathedral is the city’s most striking landmark. It as if shows the visitor where the city centre is.
The cathedral does not only dominate due to its impressive height (the apex of the tower reaches 70 meters) but also because of its convenient and well-chosen location.
The construction of the new church started around 1617. It is considered that it was initiated by the Samogitian bishop Mikalojus Pacas, while the key sponsor was the governor of Šiauliai Crown Estate Jeronimas Valavičius. Construction works were led by the dean of the church, the graduate of Vilnius Academy Petras Tarvainis.
On October 8, 1634, the bishop of Samogitia Jurgis Tiškevičius consecrated the new church of Šiauliai. Thanks to these people, a meaningful epithet “the greatest in all Samogitia”, describing the beauty and majesty of the church’s architecture, was heard on the lips of the Samogitian bishop Motiejus Valančius in later centuries.
Interestingly, the church tower had a mechanical clock installed for the money of the city residents.
The image of the architectural monument of the 17 century slightly changed over time. Wars and storms devastated the church time and again. Every few decades the church was repaired, renovated.
Prisikėlimo Square (Resurrection Square)
The central square of the city is divided into 4 parts by Aušros Avenue and Tilžės Street. This is the place around which the city of Šiauliai started growing. For centuries, the square was used for markets, fairs, live trading.
Interestingly, this oldest square of the city, the heart of the city, did not have an official name for a long time: it used to be called just Market, Market Square. Only in 1938, the square was assigned the name Laisvė (Freedom). In 1948, it was called Pergalė (Victory). In 1998, by the
decision of Šiauliai City Council, the city’s central square was labelled Prisikėlimo (Resurrection) in the honour of the Resurrection District of the Lithuanian partisans’ resistance, to which Šiauliai partisans also belonged. The square symbolizes the resurrection of the nation.

Ahora tengo una imagen clara: Vilniaus gatvė y Tilžės gatvė son las dos calles principales perpendiculares de Šiauliai, que se cruzan en la plaza central (Prisikėlimo aikštė). La calle Vilniaus va de este a oeste, y Tilžės de sur a norte. El edificio grande en el fondo de la foto podría ser la catedral de San Pedro y San Pablo que domina el centro.

La postal de eBay mencionaba "Bolschaja-Straße (Большая)" que podría ser el nombre ruso de Vilniaus gatvė. Voy a verificar la ubicación con Street View.

trace.content:
Puedo ver claramente la Catedral de San Pedro y San Pablo al sur de la plaza (en el heading=180°). La ciudad fue completamente reconstruida después de la WWI (85% destruida), así que los edificios actuales no van a coincidir con la foto de 1915. Sin embargo, la estructura urbana básica (las calles perpendiculares) se mantiene.

La foto muestra tropas marchando por una calle con tiendas a la derecha. El eBay snippet decía que era en la intersección con Bolshaya Street. Necesito determinar si "Bolshaya" era el nombre ruso de Vilniaus gatvė o de Tilžės. Voy a buscar más sobre los nombres rusos de las calles de Šiauliai.

Šiauliai 1917
A postcard of Schaulen, now Šiauliai, Lithuania during the World War I German occupation. Posted from the Feldpost (Field post station) of the 78th Reserve Division (83rd Batallion)which is believed to be active between 1915 and 1917 around Šiauliai and Panevėžys, along with the Feldpost station 175.
Acquired in 2007 in Dresden, Germany.
This postcard has been posted by the Kriegslazarett, which is a military hospital of the battlefield. The purple stamp shows that it was the Kriegslazarett Abteilung (department)124, which was stationed in Šiauliai (Schaulen). The sender adressed it to the Feldpost station 175.
Acquired in 2010 on Ebay Germany.

El blog confirma la actividad del 78th Reserve Division en Šiauliai entre 1915-1917 durante la ocupación alemana. Ahora tengo bastante evidencia para confirmar que la foto es de Šiauliai (Schaulen), Lituania, durante la ocupación alemana de la WWI, probablemente en julio de 1915 cuando las tropas alemanas entraron a la ciudad.

Ahora necesito determinar la calle exacta. El snippet de eBay decía "eine der Hauptstraßen der Stadt an der Kreuzung mit der Bolschaja-Straße (Большая)". Busquemos qué calle era "Bolshaya" en Šiauliai.

trace.content:
No veo una entrada específica sobre "Vilniaus Street" en las historias de calles, pero sí veo que hay varias calles con nombres rusos pre-WWI. Nota que "Vilenskaya" era el nombre ruso de la calle que conecta con Vilnius. Necesito buscar cuál era el nombre "Bolshaya" (Grande) en Šiauliai. Podría ser la actual Vilniaus gatvė.

Ya tengo suficiente evidencia para hacer mi hipótesis: la foto muestra tropas alemanas marchando por Šiauliai en julio de 1915. Basándome en el snippet de eBay que describía exactamente esta escena en "eine der Hauptstraßen der Stadt an der Kreuzung mit der Bolschaja-Straße", la ubicación es cerca de la plaza central de Šiauliai, en la intersección de las calles principales.

Voy a buscar una ubicación más precisa mirando la calle Vilniaus gatvė a nivel de calle.

trace.content:
Esta es la actual Vilniaus gatvė (ahora peatonal) en Šiauliai. Los edificios actuales son completamente diferentes de los de 1915 porque el 85% de la ciudad fue destruido en la WWI. Sin embargo, el trazado de la calle se mantiene.

Ahora tengo suficiente evidencia para confirmar mi hipótesis. El snippet de eBay describía exactamente una postal de "Deutsche Soldaten marschieren in Schaulen (Šiauliai), Litauen, Juli 1915" en "eine der Hauptstraßen der Stadt an der Kreuzung mit der Bolschaja-Straße". Esto coincide perfectamente con mi foto: soldados alemanes con Pickelhaube marchando por una calle principal con tiendas con carteles en ruso pre-revolucionario (МАГАЗИНЪ).

Voy a submitir mi respuesta con las coordenadas del centro de Šiauliai, cerca de la intersección de las calles principales.

answer.location: Šiauliai (Schaulen), Lithuania - calle principal (Vilniaus gatvė / Bolshaya ulitsa), centro de la ciudad
answer.reasoning: La foto muestra una columna de soldados alemanes con cascos Pickelhaube marchando por una calle de una ciudad con carteles de tiendas en ruso pre-revolucionario (incluyendo "МАГАЗИНЪ" con el signo duro ъ). trace.content:
Excelentes hallazgos. La celda 14 muestra "Schaulen - Kathedralenstraße" y tiene un estilo arquitectónico muy similar a la foto target. Los edificios de ladrillo y madera con tiendas en planta baja son muy parecidos. Sin embargo, la foto target muestra una calle diferente - quizá no sea Šiauliai, o es otra calle de la misma ciudad. 

Pero también noto que 85% de Šiauliai fue destruido en abril 1915. La foto target muestra edificios intactos, así que podría ser: (1) otra ciudad lituana, (2) Šiauliai antes de la destrucción (pero los soldados están ya marchando), o (3) una parte de Šiauliai que no fue destruida.

Consideremos también otras ciudades: Kaunas (Kowno), Panevėžys, Vilnius, o incluso ciudades en la actual Polonia o Bielorrusia. Los carteles en ruso sugieren que era territorio del Imperio Ruso.

Voy a buscar más ampliamente, quizás enfocándome en otras ciudades lituanas o del frente oriental.

trace.content:
Encontré una postal del Herder-Institut mostrando "468. Kowno - Beim Einzug der deutschen Truppen" (Kaunas - Entrada de las tropas alemanas). La postal muestra una calle de Kaunas con carteles en ruso (cirílico). La arquitectura tiene similitudes con la foto target. Sin embargo, no es exactamente la misma escena. En la postal del Herder hay caballería, mientras que en mi foto hay infantería marchando en columna.

Pero hay varias postales del "Einzug" alemán en diferentes ciudades lituanas. Necesito considerar más opciones. Veo que hay postales de Vilnius (Wilna) también mostrando la entrada de la infantería alemana. También Panevėžys (Panevys). Voy a investigar más.

Šiauliai
Hallo! Ich heiße Anastasija!
Ich möchte  Ihnen etwas über die litauische Stadt Šiauliai erzählen.
Sie wurde
1236
zum ersten Mal schriftlich erwähnt.
Meine Mutter ist hier geboren und aufgewachsen.
Šiauliai im 19. Jahrhundert
D
er Name der Stadt Šiauliai kommt entweder vom litauischen Wort „
Saulė
“
(die Sonne) oder vom Wort „
Šaulys
“ (der Schütze).
Die Stadt Šiauliai liegt im
Norden Litauens,
in der Nähe der Grenze zu Lettland. Es gibt
den
See Rekiva
nicht weit von der Stadt.
Es gibt
100 653
Einwohner in
Šiauliai.
Stadtgeschichte
das Wappen von Šiauliai
1791
erhielt Šiauliai die Magdeburger Rechte und ein Wappen.
1795
wurde Litauen von Russland annektiert. Katharina II. schenkte die Stadt dem Fürsten Platon Zubow.
1897
wurde Šiauliai die zweitgrößte Stadt Litauens.
Mehr als die Hälfte der litauischen Gebäude wurden während des Ersten Weltkriegs zerstört.
Während des Zweiten Weltkriegs wurde die Stadt bombardiert.
Sehenswürdigkeiten
Der Berg der Kreuze
Der Berg der Kreuze.
Es ist ein kleiner Hügel. Er liegt 12 km von Šiauliai. Darauf befinden sich
etwa 60 Tausend Kreuze
(meist katholisch, aber nicht nur). Hier kann man ein Kreuz aufstellen. Dieser Berg bringt Glück.
Goldjunge
Goldjunge.
Im Zentrum des Platzes steht ein
4 Meter hoher Schütze,
der Goldjunge.
Auf dem Platz ist eine Sonnenuhr mit
den Zahlen 3, 6 und 12 zu sehen
.
Sie stellen das Jahr 1236 dar.
Sie ist die höchste Sonnenuhr in Litauen.
Kathedrale der Heiligen Peter und Paul
Die St.
Peter und Paul -
Kathedrale.
Die Kirche wurde im
siebzehnten Jahrhundert
im Stil der Renaissance erbaut. Sie
ist weiß mit einem roten Ziegeldach. D
er Turm ist
70 Meter hoch
.
Die Unternehmen
Die Süßwarenfabrik Ruta
Süßwarenfabrik "Ruta".
"Ruta" ist eine litauische Süßwarenfabrik mit der längsten Geschichte. Sie
ist
1912
gegründet.
Die Geschäfte der Marke Ruta sind in den größten Städten Litauens geöffnet.
Im historischen Gebäude der Fabrik wurde ein
Schokoladenmuseum
geöffnet.
Die Fahrradfabrik "Vairas"
Die Fahrradfabrik "Vairas" ("Lenkrad"
).
1980
wurde auf dem Gelände der alten Fabrik ein Fahrradmuseum errichtet.
Marija
Lastauskaite
Marija
Lastauskaite
Maria Lastauskaite ist eine litauische Schrifstellerin. Sie ist besser bekannt unter dem Pseudonym
Lazdynu Peleda (Waldeule).
Sie wurde 1872 geboren. S
ie ist die erste Feministin in Litauen.
Ihr Ehemann ist der belarussische Schriftsteller
Vaclav Lastovsky.
Mein Lieblingsort in der Stadt
Mein Lieblingsort in der Stadt ist der Spielplatz in der Nähe des Hauses meines Großvaters.
Als Kind habe ich hier mit meiner Schwester im Sandkasten gespielt und Eis gegessen.
Es gibt eine große Holzschaukel. In der Nähe des Hauses wachsen viele Linden.
Das letzte Mal war ich dieses Jahr dort.
Heute ist diese Stadt menschenleer. Junge Leute gehen nach Vilnius oder in andere Länder. Aber ich fahre immer wieder gerne in diese Stadt. Ich hoffe, sie hat Ihnen auch gefallen!

trace.content:
Interesante. La primera imagen muestra "Szavle - Avenue de la Police" con la catedral de San Pedro y San Pablo al fondo. La arquitectura de esa postal tiene similitudes con la foto target - edificios de ladrillo de 2-3 pisos con tiendas en planta baja. Pero no es la misma calle exacta.

Ahora voy a reconsiderar. La foto target muestra una columna de infantería alemana marchando por una calle principal. La ciudad tiene carteles en ruso (ortografía pre-revolucionaria). Podría ser cualquier ciudad del antiguo Imperio Ruso ocupada por Alemania en 1915. Pero el 85% de Šiauliai fue destruido en abril 1915, y en la foto los edificios están intactos. Esto sugiere que o bien es otra ciudad, o es una parte de Šiauliai que sobrevivió.

Déjame buscar más específicamente, quizás otras ciudades como Panevėžys o ciudades más pequeñas.

The first 2 postcards were sent from Poniewiesz/Poniewiez, now called Panevėžys, Lithuania, on 1915 from the fielpost station 175. trace.content:
Muy interesante. La postal de "Poniewiez. Markt" (Panevėžys - Mercado) muestra una calle con arquitectura MUY similar a la foto target - edificios de ladrillo de 2-3 pisos con tiendas, carteles en ruso (veo "АПТЕКА Б. СУБОЦКАГО" - Farmacia de B. Subotsky). La mezcla de edificios de ladrillo y madera es muy parecida.

Sin embargo, la postal muestra que Panevėžys fue "durch Russen in Trümmer gelegt" (destruida por los rusos). La foto target muestra los edificios intactos.

Ahora debo considerar: ¿la foto target podría ser de Panevėžys ANTES de la destrucción, al momento de la llegada de las tropas alemanas? O ¿es otra ciudad que no fue destruida?

Voy a buscar más específicamente si hay fotos del Einmarsch (entrada) de tropas alemanas en Panevėžys o ciudades similares.

Basándome en toda la investigación que he hecho, tengo bastante evidencia para concluir que esta foto es del frente oriental de la WWI, mostrando tropas alemanas marchando por una ciudad lituana. Las ciudades candidatas principales son Šiauliai, Panevėžys, Kaunas, o Vilnius.

Mirando la arquitectura más cuidadosamente: los edificios en la foto target tienen una mezcla de ladrillo y madera, con tiendas en planta baja y carteles en ruso. La ciudad no parece ser tan grande como Vilnius o Kaunas (que tenían edificios más imponentes). La similitud con la postal de Panevėžys (Poniewiez. Markt) es notable.

Sin embargo, dado que no puedo identificar la ciudad exacta con certeza absoluta, voy a buscar directamente la postal de la foto - quizás tiene texto o una descripción que identifique el lugar.

Fotografen Fritz Theodor Benzen (1864-1945) var uddannet boghandler og havde i perioden 1891-1906 forretning i Købmagergade, senere i Frederiksberggade og fra 1917 i Sølvgade. Her solgte han billeder og postkort, som han formodentligt selv havde fotograferet. Samtidig fotograferede han også mange af de bygninger, der stadig præger Københavns gadebillede i dag, og som vidner om både historisk bevidsthed såvel som en personlig fascination over at se en by under markant forandring.

Es la Белая Башня (Torre Blanca) de Ekaterimburgo, diseñada por el arquitecto Moiseí Reisher y construida entre 1929-1931 como torre de agua para el socgorod (ciudad socialista) del complejo industrial Uralmash (УЗТМ). La foto muestra la torre recién completada: el entorno está sin urbanizar, hay troncos de madera en primer plano (desmonte del bosque para la construcción), y el bosque de coníferas rodea la estructura. La torre tiene 29 metros de altura y fue uno de los primeros edificios de hormigón armado de Sverdlovsk (hoy Ekaterimburgo).

No 59 started as a chemist in 1859. It was Robert Morris, followed by Sales and Nurse in 1900, then Edwin. C. Corkhill in 1932. In 1967 T. B. Small and in 2000 A. S. Wren pharmacy was in residence and finally Boots took over. In 2012 it closed.
Excellent example of an old chemist shop. With some great restoration
Architecture
CREDIT Joe Thompson 2023
In 1720, the land on which Nos. 50-59A and No. 60 now stand was a single property held by William Mewse ( butcher) and his wife Anne - being described as a messuage with a yard and fish-houses. The Manor Roll of 1618 names Thomas Powell as occupant, with tenants called Killet and Holland preceding him. The Mewses were a long established family of butchers in the town, with roots going back to the Lay Subsidy of 1568.
One entry in the Lowestoft manorial records just happens to reveal that an earlier house on the plot, belonging to Thomas Arnold (mariner), had been destroyed in the fire of 10 March 1645. The blaze gutted all the fish-houses on Whapload Road from the site of the former No. 1 High Street as far as Rant Score (seventeen -eighteen buildings) and destroyed or seriously damaged the houses (twelve in all) along the east side of the High Street on land now occupied by Nos. 47-63. It also jumped across the roadway and similarly affected Nos. 143 to 148-9 on the west side and two houses behind them (seven dwellings, in all).
Thomas Arnold's loss of dwelling fish-houses and goods was put at £375 13s 0d and the damage overall was estimated at £10,297 2s 4d. It took the town many years to recover from this event and it was the worst fire to have been recorded during the town's pre-industrial history.
CREDIT:David Butcher
ArchitectureListing
* as a rare and intelligible example of a purpose built mid-Victorian chemist shop and house; * for the rare and complete survival of the original shopfront; * as an early example of an Italianate style shopfront, particularly suited to chemist shops; * for the wealth of internal fixtures and fittings, dating from construction to the mid-C20, reflecting the evolution of the chemist shop;
Historic Interest:
* as a building which remained in use as a chemist for around 161 years and clearly reflects its history and evolution within its fabric;
Group value:
* as one of numerous listed buildings along the High Street which contribute to the character of Lowestoft High Street and stand testament to its Victorian prosperity.
History
The name Lowestoft is Scandinavian in origin and may be translated as Hloover’s toft – the homestead of Hloover. The town relocated to the cliff-top from an earlier site, about a mile to the south-west, during the period 1300-1350, partly because of increasing maritime activity (especially herring-fishing) and the need it created to be closer to the sea, and partly because of the difficulty of accommodating an expanding population in-situ without building houses on valuable agricultural land. The area chosen for the new site was low-grade coastal heath, used mainly for the rough-grazing of livestock which became a more useful asset to the manorial lord as building-land. The main street is of sinuous alignment, following the natural curves of the cliff. The better-off members of the community lived along the High Street whilst the less affluent largely resided in a gridiron side-street area to the west. Lowestoft was thus a planned late medieval town.
The High Street was lined with burgage plots containing prosperous merchants’ houses for much of the medieval and early modern period, and the cliff-face was made usable by terracing. The cliff-top itself provided an area behind the houses for the storage of household goods and materials; and the first step down was multi-purpose, sometimes planted with fruit trees and used as an amenity area, but also functioning as a place for putting all kinds of household waste. The second and third stages down were mainly taken up with the buildings that serviced fishing and other maritime enterprise: curing-houses, net-stores, stables and the like. Access from the cliff-top to the sea was provided by footways known as scores (three of them widened for use by carts) – a word deriving from the Old Norse ‘skora’, meaning ‘to cut’ or ‘to incise’. These had originally started life as surface-water gullies down the soft face of the cliff – a natural process that lent itself to use as tracks.
The chief trade of Lowestoft and the source of its prosperity remained herring fishing until the C19. Then in 1827 the harbour was created, and in 1832 the navigation continued through to Oulton Broad, giving access to the River Waveney and Norwich. Samuel Morton Peto was brought in to construct the outer harbour, and he ensured the arrival of the railway in 1847 as well as developing the land south of the harbour as a seaside resort. The town was bombarded by the Germans in 1916 and suffered considerable damage from 178 enemy raids in the Second World War. Post-war reconstruction involved new roads being cut through the northern part of the town. In the later years of the C20 the fishing industry has almost completely declined.
An internal inspection of the 59-59A High Street for the purposes of this listing assessment was not possible. However, a research investigation of the building carried out between May and August 2018 by Historic England (Morrison 2018, see sources), provides an up to date account of the building and has provided the factual details for both the History and Details sections of this report. A greater level of detail is available in the original Research Report.
In June 1851 it was reported that the former premises of the National Provincial Bank in Lowestoft were in the process of being rebuilt for the proprietor, a Mr. Morris, Chemist. Relatively little is known of Morris’s early life. He was born in the village of Cratfield, near Halesworth in Suffolk on 25th April 1811 to William and Mary Morris, his father being a farmer. In 1841 he lived with Thomas Morris, 15, and Hannah Morris, 15, presumably siblings or cousins who assisted with the business and housekeeping. He married in 1841.
Morris was undoubtedly trading as a chemist on Lowestoft High Street by 1839, when he was listed in Pigot and Co’s Directory. Shortly before this, he may have had some kind of business association with a Lowestoft chemist named Robert Smith, who later became his brother-in-law. Robert Smith, chemist, advertised for an apprentice (‘a well-educated youth’) in county newspapers in March 1839. Smith and Morris married daughters of the fish merchant William Cleveland, who owned no 59 High Street until 1850.
Smith quit Lowestoft in 1839 to open a chemist shop in Colchester and in April 1839 Morris took over a property that had been occupied by Samuel Sharman Brame (1813-63), who was a qualified surgeon as well as a chemist. Brame continued to run a chemist’s shop on the High Street, but may have moved to new premises in 1839. Certainly his business continued to exist in tandem with Morris’s.
Lettering on the edge of the carboy shelf in the window of Morris’s shop front reads: ‘FAMILY DISPENSING CHEMIST EST. 1817’. There was no shop of any kind at No. 59 High Street prior to 1851, and so this must refer to the foundation of the business at a different address. A connection probably existed between Morris and some other chemist, druggist, apothecary or surgeon trading in Lowestoft before 1839, but this has not been traced. A cupboard door surviving in the shop at No. 59 High Street, painted with the arms of the Society of Apothecaries, may be a remnant from the early years of this business. The Morris family retained ownership of 59 High Street but by 1873 the business had passed to Mr William J Riches, a young chemist who had previously, in 1861, lived on Denmark Street. However, in 1873 Riches went bankrupt, his whole stock-in-trade was sold at auction and the shop was quickly taken on by another chemist, Thomas John Sale (1848-89).
In 1882 59 High Street was sold by Morris’s heirs. The building was bought by James Edwin Hart, an ironmonger in Clare, Suffolk but the business continued to be run by Sale until his death in 1889. Sale also ran a branch establishment in South Street, Clapham Road, Lowestoft. Sale’s widow was still residing at no. 59 High Street, ‘living on her own means’ with her household. This included Sale’s former assistant, James A. Nurse, who had been approached by Sale’s executors to run the business which was consequently renamed Sale and Nurse. Nurse purchased the premises from Hart's Son in 1893.
Nurse continued to run the chemist as ‘Sale and Nurse’ and lived above the shop with his wife Helen. When he died in 1924 the business was taken over by Edwin Christian Corkhill, who continued to sell ‘Nurse’s Cough Linctus’. Corkhill bought the premises from Helen Nurse in 1936, although he lived elsewhere. A ghost sign on the north gable wall of No.59 High Street relates to Corkhill's tenure.
Although having changed hands several times through mid to late-C20 the property continued to function as an independent chemist shop until 2000 when it became an Alliance Pharmacy. In 2006 Alliance UniChem merged with Boots, and in 2009 the shop was rebranded as Boots. The company announced closure in 2012 and the property was sold to the current owners.

29 High Street This substantial property was built as a house in 1858 and was inhabited by John C. Kell until 1863. James Butcher a boat owner who lived there until 1883 succeeded him. Between 1883 and 1892 it was merged with 30 High Street and was run as a ladies school run by Miss Emma Elizabeth Smith as headmistress. In 1892 it was converted into offices the first occupier being Herbert Frederick Smith, a collector of income and property taxes. George Stonham Tasker, the deputy clerk to St. Margaret’s parish church lived here between 1896 and 1900 In 1900 29 High Street was re-converted into a house and was inhabited by James Franklin Edwards until 1910, Ralph Foort between 1910 and 1922 and Mrs. Jean Dale between 1922 and 1947. In 1947 Robert Dale converted part of the property to set up in business as a boot repairer going into partnership as Dales Bros boot repairers in 1959. In 1973 the property was converted back into a house being inhabited by Alfred and Dorothy Coggle. They lived here until 1982 when Elsie Baker inhabited it until 1984 followed by Gordon and Marie Bush until 1988. Between 1988 and 1993, 29 High Street was converted into 5 flats after which Denise and Tony Meades converted it back into a house.
As you can see from the plaque, the house was once the home of the Allin Family, after that point the front of the house had a shop window and door and from 1900 to the late 1960's it was Dale Brothers, Boot and Shoe Repairs. No. 29 High Street is the rebuilt northern half of a former single dwelling, with No. 30 being the southern section - the whole of which once belonged to the Allen/Allin family (the surname being found in both forms). Robert Allen (merchant) is named as tenant in the Manor Roll of 1618. He was the father of the famous Restoration-period naval commander, Sir Thomas Allin, who was born in November 1612. A century later, in 1720, the property was held - in the right of his wife - by William Balls (merchant), who owned two fishing vessels involved in catching herring and mackerel. The building is described as being of freehold tenure and divided into two tenements, with a bake house and yard attached. The earliest record of tenure is that of William Davy (merchant) in February 1584.
At some point, after Robert Allen's occupancy, the property came into the tenure of the Jenkenson family - though no record of this is to be found. In October 1658, Henry Jenkenson was admitted to it, by terms of his brother Edward's will. After this, no further details of transfer are to be found.
About 80-85% of Lowestoft's housing stock was held by copyhold tenure, whereby the lord of the manor was paid an annual ground-rent by the tenants, as well as an entry fine (as it was called) by new, incoming tenants every time a property changed hands. All transfers were supposed to be recorded by the steward of the manor in the court baron minute books - but some did escape attention. Freehold properties did not have to have their changes in occupancy noted.
When he retired from the Royal Navy in 1672, Sir Thomas Allin purchased the manorial titles of both Lowestoft and Somerleyton and took up residence in the latter place's Hall. It looks likely that he sold the freehold of Nos. 29-30 to Henry Jenkenson, which accounts for there being no details of transfer after 1668. He died in 1685, so the transaction must have taken place between 1672 and that year.

House. C16 origins, but so altered that no features of that date remain. Present character is C20. Re-built mid C19. Rendered and colourwashed brick. Concrete corrugated roof tiles. 2 storeys and attic in one bay. Plank panelled door to the right and left, both under plain overlights. The left-hand door formerly led to a passageway to rear. One late C20 Venetian window lights ground floor. One late C20 top-hung casement to upper floor. Gabled roof with a rendered and reduced internal north gable-end stack. C19 extensions to the rear, now lit through C20 casements. Rear terrace built 1940 as a bofors gun platform. INTERIOR. Stick baluster staircase, the balusters replaced late C20. Ramped handrail mid C19. One 2-panel C18 door remains to first floor. Included for group value.
